voice_event.text:
Jesus is the Only-Begotten, the Ihidaya - our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. To us he is the one who fulfilled every old promise: our Nativity hymns sing of the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad, because what they had carried forward came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom - and his own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him.

Most of all, he is the Physician. One of our teachers put it this way: of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. He came as medicine for a wounded people.

We sang him more than we defined him. What we held about him, we held in hymns first.

glosses.plain_meaning: The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.
glosses.quick_meaning: The Single One: our word for the vowed celibate - and, at the same time, our title for Christ the Only-Begotten.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Solitary' misleads: the ihidaye lived among the congregation, not in isolation; the singleness is of heart and allegiance, not of address.

voice_event.text:
He broke into death's kingdom. Our hymns stage it as rescue and invasion both: Death himself trembles, complaining that Jesus has plundered his house. Since Adam, death had ruled everyone without distinction - that was the world he entered. He took sin and nailed it to his cross. Then he went down into Sheol, the silent country where all the dead go, and came back out. Our poet sang it this way: Sin and Hell were terrified. Death trembled, and the dead revived.

His rising is the pledge given to mortals that Sheol gives back its dead. What he did was open a door that had been shut since the beginning. And he healed. The sage taught that he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for the wound everyone carries. We held that he does not reject the one who repents - the only thing that keeps a wound from healing is the shame that hides it.

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

The word comes from the root yhd, which carries the sense of being one, alone, or singular. Among us, the ihidaye are the men and women of the covenant - the qyama - who vowed themselves to a celibate life for good. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation. And the same name we gave them is the name we gave to Jesus: the Only-Begotten who left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
We believed Jesus is the Only-Begotten because we received the witness, tested it in how we lived, and found it true in what happened to us. The Gospel came to us as one continuous story - the harmony our churches read in worship. We had no living eyewitnesses; a century and more stood between us and the events. What we had was preaching received and argument tested.

And we believed it because of what it did. On the Persian side, believers staked their lives on him under a hostile crown. When a debater taunted one of our teachers - if your faith were true, wouldn't your prayers have stopped the killing? - the teacher answered from Scripture, not by claiming rescue had come. The whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead. Our own poet sang: Sin and Hell were terrified, Death trembled, and the dead revived.

We believed because people we knew gave everything for it, and because the story made sense of a world where death rules everyone and only One had broken into that country and come back out.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
Jacob of Nisibis lived it out as a bishop who held his city when the empire could not. He stood at the great council in Nicaea in 325, one bishop among three hundred, when the church named its faith against those who would divide the Son from the Father. Then he came home to a fortress-city on the frontier, and when the Persian king laid siege to it, the tradition remembers him praying on the walls. Three times Shapur came against Nisibis while Jacob lived, and three times the city held.

What Jacob lived was steadiness. Our own hymns sing of him as the city's father, one of three bishops - Jacob, Babu, Valgash - who prayed for Nisibis and taught it what it believed. Office was real among us, and he held it. But his standing came as much from being found trustworthy over time as from being made a bishop. He shepherded a congregation that knew rival teachers by name - Bardaisan's songs were still sung in Edessa, Marcion's followers still gathered, and we held our faith by answering theirs out loud. Jacob's life, as far as our record shows it, was spent keeping one city faithful and standing.

results.message: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?

voice_event.speaker: syr
voice_event.text:
That the way we knew Jesus was not the way a court hears a case. We did not argue from archives or prove it from living memory - we had neither. What we had was a received witness, sung and lived, and we tested it in how people carried their days and, on the Persian side, in how they died. The whole community staked itself on the risen Lord as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead.

And we knew what we believed by answering, out loud, the neighbors who taught otherwise. Bardaisan's followers were still in Edessa two hundred years after his death. Marcion's congregations shared our streets. Mani's new religion sent its teachers through the same cities we lived in. Holding the faith rightly among us was not a settled inheritance - it was an ongoing act of telling truth apart from a plausible-sounding neighbor.

One of our own teachers, notably, stood closer to us than the others. With Bardaisan we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us, and free will is God's gift. Where we parted from him was on whether God made all things from nothing, and on the body's resurrection. The arguments happened in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against people everyone knew by name.
